opus-5.5.text:
I think it helps to separate two questions that often get blurred together. One is: what does the robot's body look like? The other is: what does the "brain" actually need to understand about the world to act well in it?

When people say "general brain," sometimes they imagine a single model that you can drop into any robot—a humanoid, a quadruped, a robot arm on a table, a drone—and it just works. I think that's a nice long-term aspiration, but in practice the body is not a neutral container. The physical configuration determines what actions are even possible, what the robot sees from its own viewpoint, how contact happens, how errors show up. So the brain and the body are coupled. A policy that's learned on a parallel-jaw gripper doesn't automatically know what to do with a five-fingered hand, because the space of things the hand can do is just fundamentally different.

That said, I don't think this means generality is hopeless. What I'd argue is that there are layers. At the higher level—understanding the scene, knowing what objects are, what the task is, what a reasonable sequence of steps looks like—a lot of that can be shared across embodiments. A cup is a cup whether you pick it up with a gripper or a hand. Then at the lower level, the actual motor control, the contact-rich interaction, that's where embodiment really matters, and I think you either need embodiment-specific adaptation or a model that has seen enough diversity of bodies that it can infer how to use a new one.

So for the choice of physical configuration, my view is that you shouldn't pick the body only because it looks general—like "humanoids are general because the world is built for humans." That's partly true, but there's a cost: more degrees of freedom, harder to control, harder to collect data for. Sometimes a simpler body that you can get a lot of high-quality data on will actually give you a more capable brain sooner, because data is really the bottleneck. And the hardware also has to be reliable and cheap enough that you can deploy it widely and close the loop—collect data, improve the model, deploy again.

So in short: I see the "general brain" less as something body-agnostic and more as something that's learned across many bodies and many tasks, where the shared understanding sits on top, and the body-specific competence sits underneath. And the choice of configuration should be driven by what lets you get that data flywheel going, not just by what looks most general on paper.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes shared higher-level abilities within tasks from embodiment-specific motor control, and contrasts a single model working across different bodies with configuration-specific competence.

r002.rationale: It explicitly includes humanoids among the different robot bodies a general model might work on, and discusses generality learned across many bodies.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the phrase “general brain” gets used a bit loosely, so let me say what I actually mean by it, and then why I think it's inseparable from the question of hardware.

When people say “general brain,” they usually imagine something like a large language model, but for the physical world: one model that you can drop into any robot, and it just works. I don't think that's quite the right picture. A brain that has never been attached to a body doesn't actually know anything about the world in the way that matters for robotics. What it knows is a kind of abstract, averaged description of the world. What a robot needs is to know what happens when *this* arm, with *this* gripper, with *this* amount of compliance, pushes against *that* object. The gap between those two things is exactly the gap between intelligence and embodiment.

So to me, a general brain is not a brain that is independent of configuration. It's a brain that has learned, across enough configurations, how to quickly adapt to a new one. Generality is about the speed of adaptation, not about the absence of a body. It's the difference between a person who has only ever driven one car and a person who has driven many different vehicles. The second person still needs a minute to adjust when you hand them something new, but a minute is enough.

And that reframing changes how you think about choosing a form factor. There are really two schools of thought. One says: pick a body that is as close to human as possible, because the world is built for humans, and all the data we have is from humans. The other says: pick the body that is cheapest and most reliable to deploy right now, because the thing you actually lack is data from real deployment, and a robot that's sitting in a lab generates zero data.

I'm actually fairly sympathetic to both, and I think the honest answer is that the configuration choice is not a scientific question so much as a bet about where the data will come from. If you believe the brain learns primarily from human video and simulation, then the humanoid form makes a lot of sense, because it minimizes the transfer gap. If you believe the brain learns primarily from robots doing real tasks in real environments, then you want the body that will be in the most places, doing the most things, as soon as possible, even if it looks nothing like a person.

My own view is that the body is a kind of curriculum. Every configuration teaches the brain certain things and hides others. A wheeled base with two arms teaches you a lot about manipulation and almost nothing about balance. A humanoid teaches you about whole-body coordination but is so hard to keep upright that you spend a huge fraction of your effort just not falling down. So I don't think there's one right choice. I think the question is: which curriculum gets you to the most valuable capabilities fastest, given the resources you have?

And the last thing I'd say is that I think the field is going to converge toward something more like how biology handles it. Nature didn't build one body and one brain. It built many bodies and the brain structure co-evolved with each of them. But the underlying learning mechanism, the thing that lets a creature figure out its own body, is quite shared. That shared mechanism is what I'd actually call the general brain. The specific body is a parameter you pass in.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a brain that supposedly works across robot types with one that adapts across configurations, but it does not distinguish that from general capabilities within a single configuration.

r002.rationale: It describes a shared learning mechanism that adapts to new configurations and explicitly discusses humanoid robots as one such configuration, including when that form makes sense.

astra-6.text:
I think a general brain should be able to work across different robot bodies, but that doesn’t mean the physical configuration is irrelevant. The body determines what the robot can perceive and do—where its sensors are, how its joints move, what it can reach, and how much force it can apply.

So I would separate two things: the ability to understand a task and reason about it, which should be broadly shared, and the ability to execute it through a particular body, which requires adaptation. A wheeled robot and a humanoid might understand the same instruction, but they’ll carry it out differently.

The choice of configuration should therefore start with the application. What environment does the robot need to work in, and what tasks must it perform? A general brain should make it easier to transfer capabilities between configurations, rather than require every robot to have the same shape.

r001.rationale: It separates task understanding from body-specific execution, but does not distinguish the two meanings of “general brain” as generality within one configuration versus applicability across multiple configurations.

r002.rationale: It says a general brain should work across different robot bodies and gives a humanoid and a wheeled robot as examples.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should separate two questions: what can be shared across robots, and what depends on the robot’s body. A general brain doesn’t necessarily mean every robot has the same physical configuration. It means there is a common foundation for understanding the environment, interpreting tasks, and planning actions, while the execution is adapted to each body’s capabilities.

For example, a wheeled robot and a humanoid might both understand “bring me that cup,” but they have different ways of reaching it, grasping it, and moving through the room. The brain has to know those differences. So generality cannot mean ignoring the body.

My view is that the physical configuration should follow the application. If wheels and one arm can do the job reliably, that may be the right choice. If the task requires navigating spaces and using tools designed for people, a humanoid configuration may have advantages. The goal is to share as much intelligence as possible while making good use of the particular body.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes capabilities shared across robots from body-dependent execution, but does not identify general capabilities within a single robot configuration as a separate meaning of “general brain.”

r002.rationale: It explicitly says a common brain can serve both wheeled robots and humanoids, including that they can understand the same task.
